The concept presupposes a collective body with authority to evaluate and discipline private sexuality — an institutional structure without a Western equivalent.

definition: Moral decay or decomposition of customs; the Soviet and conservative Russian phrase for the decline of sexual and social morality, typically attributed to Western capitalist influence, permissiveness, or deliberate ideological subversion.
notes: Разложение means decomposition or putrefaction, applied to нравы (customs/mores); the metaphor frames sexual permissiveness as biological rot. Standard Soviet ideological formulation used to condemn homosexuality, pornography, and rock music alike; still deployed by Russian Orthodox Church spokespeople.

definition: Anti-social behavior; the Soviet legal and moral catch-all phrase applied to behaviors deemed harmful to socialist society, including homosexuality, prostitution, public drunkenness, and sexual promiscuity.
notes: In Soviet law, male homosexuality was classified under this category alongside hooliganism until Russia decriminalized it in 1993. The phrase remains in active conservative and legal discourse as a condemnation of sexual nonconformity; approximate match only because the English phrase lacks the Soviet legal-punitive weight.

definition: Soviet moral-legal category meaning 'social parasitism' — living without socially useful labor — deployed against those whose lifestyles (including sex workers and homosexuals) were deemed incompatible with socialist norms.
notes: Primarily a work-ethics and ideological term, not intrinsically sexual; included in sexuality indices because it was used to prosecute prostitutes, gay men, and the sexually dissolute under the 1961 anti-parasitism decree. Joseph Brodsky was famously convicted under it. Recognition higher among adults 40+ who lived under the Soviet system.

definition: Sexual licentiousness or moral looseness; a condemnatory compound phrase used in both Soviet official discourse and Orthodox moral teaching to denounce unrestrained sexual behavior.
notes: Распущенность alone means 'lack of discipline/moral looseness'; the compound specifies the sexual domain. Stilted and formal — never street slang. Heard in official speeches, church homilies, and moralizing journalism.

definition: Free love; the early-Soviet revolutionary ideology, most associated with Alexandra Kollontai, that rejected bourgeois marriage as a property institution and advocated sexual relationships based on desire and mutual consent alone.
notes: Prominent in 1917–1930 Bolshevik sexual politics before Stalin reversed course in the 1930s and reimposed conservative family norms. Now used historically, ironically, or in leftist discourse. Mapped to ethical_non_monogamy as closest concept, though free love carries an explicit anti-institutional ideological charge absent from ENM.

definition: Bourgeois morality; Marxist-Leninist shorthand for the sexual and family ethics of the capitalist class — monogamy, premarital chastity, property-based marriage — condemned in Soviet thought as ideological tools of class oppression.
notes: Ironic historical arc: early Soviets condemned bourgeois sexual conservatism, yet by the 1930s Soviet society became more sexually conservative than what it mocked. Still heard in contemporary leftist or satirical discourse. Recognition skews older.

definition: Decadentism; Soviet critical term for the perceived cultural and moral degeneration of bourgeois society, encompassing sexual permissiveness, aesthetic excess, nihilism, and despair.
notes: Derived from упадок (decline/decay). In Soviet literary criticism it targeted Symbolist and Decadent artists; in moral discourse it condemned Western sexual and cultural excess as evidence of capitalist collapse. Very low recognition among speakers under 40.

definition: Fornication or sexual immorality; in Orthodox Christian theology one of the eight capital passions, encompassing all non-marital sexual acts and regarded as a sin against God and the body.
notes: Church Slavonic root word from which блудница (harlot), блудный (prodigal/lecherous), and распутство derive. Distinct from прелюбодеяние (adultery specifically). Carries both theological weight and mild everyday crudeness — used colloquially to mean 'lechery' without religious framing.

definition: Adultery; in Orthodox theology and pre-revolutionary Russian law, sexual intercourse by a married person with someone other than their spouse — a more specific and more severely condemned sin than блуд.
notes: Strictly means adultery (violation of marital fidelity); the registry's 'fornication' concept covers pre-marital sex and is not exact. In Orthodox confession, прелюбодеяние and блуд are enumerated as distinct sins. Formal, ecclesiastical register — never colloquial.

definition: The sin of fornication or lust; a set phrase from Orthodox moral theology naming sexual immorality as a sin against both God and the temple of the body.
notes: Compound phrase: блудный (lecherous/fornicating — same root as 'prodigal' in блудный сын, the Prodigal Son) + грех (sin). Common in Orthodox confessional and homiletic contexts. Slightly higher crude score than блуд alone due to the explicit 'sin' framing intensifying the moral charge.

definition: Sinful; adjective applied in Orthodox and broader Russian cultural discourse to characterize sexual desires, thoughts, or acts as contrary to divine law and spiritually corrupting.
notes: General religious adjective. Applied to sexuality to frame desire as inherently morally suspect — e.g., греховные мысли (sinful thoughts), греховные желания (sinful desires). Widely used outside strictly religious contexts in everyday moralizing speech.

definition: Sin; in sexual contexts, the Orthodox and broader Russian cultural framing of sexual desire and non-marital sex as a transgression against divine law — the foundational moral category governing all sexuality in religious discourse.
notes: Extremely high-frequency word with many non-sexual applications. Sexual meaning is the dominant application in Orthodox moral theology, activated by collocations: грехи плоти (sins of the flesh), введение в грех (leading into sin). Mapped to carnal_desire as the closest available registry concept.

definition: Ritual and moral impurity; in Orthodox theology, a state of spiritual uncleanness caused by sexual acts, menstruation, nocturnal emission, or other bodily events, requiring prayer and abstinence before full participation in worship.
notes: Encompasses both ritual impurity (temporary, cleansable through prayer) and moral impurity (sinful). Has strong Hebrew Bible antecedents (טָמֵא / tāmēʾ) transmitted through the Septuagint. Broader and more theologically precise than the registry's 'indecency,' which implies public-decency violation rather than ritual uncleanness.

definition: Chastity or sexual purity; in Orthodox Christianity, a cardinal virtue encompassing pre-marital virginity, marital fidelity, and the disciplined subordination of sexual desire to spiritual order.
notes: Etymology: целый (whole/intact) + мудрость (wisdom) — 'wholeness of mind.' Broader than mere abstinence: it is an attitude of integrated purity governing the whole person. Highly esteemed in Orthodox monastic and lay ascetic tradition. Closer to the Latin 'castitas' than to simple virginity.

definition: Carnal sin or sin of the flesh; Orthodox phrase for any sin rooted in bodily appetite, predominantly applied to sexual transgressions.
notes: Плотский derives from плоть (flesh). Nearly interchangeable with блудный грех in common use but technically broader — can include gluttony and other physical sins — though the sexual application is overwhelmingly dominant in confessional and homiletic contexts.

definition: Sodomy; in Russian Orthodox and historical legal usage, anal intercourse or other non-procreative sexual acts, historically criminalized and strongly condemned as a sin against nature and God.
notes: Borrowed from the biblical city of Sodom via Church Slavonic and Latin. Criminalized in Russia under Soviet Article 121 until 1993. Prominently revived in contemporary Russian anti-LGBT rhetoric since 2013; recognition has risen accordingly. Carries both theological condemnation and legal-historical register.

definition: Sodomite; in Orthodox theology and traditional Russian public discourse, a man who practices anal sex — used almost exclusively as a condemnation of homosexual men.
notes: Religious-legal pejorative. Usage has intensified sharply in Russian public discourse since the 2013 'gay propaganda' law, deployed by conservative commentators and clergy as an alternative to gay/homosexual that carries maximum moral-historical condemnation. Crude score reflects its function as a slur.

definition: Harlot or fornicatrix; in Orthodox usage, a woman guilty of sexual immorality — encompassing both prostitutes and promiscuous women who commit блуд.
notes: Feminine form derived from блуд. Famous from the Gospel narrative of the sinful woman (traditionally conflated with Mary Magdalene). Distinct from проститутка (prostitute) by its theological-moral rather than transactional framing. Carries the dual sense of sexual sinner and fallen woman; the condemnation is moral, not merely commercial.

definition: Fallen woman; a 19th-century Russian literary and social euphemism for a woman who has lost her sexual virtue through seduction, coercion, or poverty-driven prostitution, framed as a social tragedy rather than purely moral condemnation.
notes: Peak in Russian realist literature: Dostoevsky's Sonya Marmeladova, Tolstoy's Katyusha Maslova. The 'fall' (падение) implies a descent from social respectability. Carries more pathos and class-critical nuance than блудница, which is purely condemnatory. The term shaped 19th-century reform movements around rescuing такие женщины.

definition: Repentance or penance; in Orthodox Christianity, the sacramental and psychological process of confessing, regretting, and committing to turn away from sexual sin — the prescribed institutional response to блуд and плотский грех.
notes: Not inherently sexual but central to Orthodox sexual ethics as the culturally enforced mechanism for processing and renouncing sexual transgression. Mapped to sexual_repression because the institutional requirement of покаяние is a primary vehicle through which Russian religious culture internalizes guilt about sexuality. Distinct from Catholic penance: Orthodox покаяние emphasizes inner transformation over prescribed acts.

definition: Spiritual delusion (prelest); in Orthodox ascetic theology, a dangerous state of self-deception where a person believes demonic or carnal temptations — including sexual ones — to be divinely inspired, leading to spiritual pride and destruction.
notes: CRITICAL DISAMBIGUATION: The common modern Russian word прелесть means 'charm/beauty/delight' (recognition ~99%) — this is an entirely different, unrelated sense. The Orthodox theological meaning documented here is known primarily by monastics, theologians, and the Orthodox educated (~28%). In ascetic texts, sexual temptation is a primary gateway into прелесть. The English transliteration 'prelest' exists in Orthodox theological writing but has no common secular equivalent. Proposed slug: orthodox_spiritual_delusion.

definition: Temptation; in sexual contexts, the experience of being drawn toward sexual sin — understood in Orthodox theology as a trial of the soul and an opportunity to choose virtue or fall into блуд.
notes: Extremely common word with many non-sexual applications (temptation to steal, to lie, etc.). Sexual temptation is the most culturally prominent application in Orthodox and general Russian religious discourse. Mapped to lust as the closest registry concept for the sexual valence, though искушение denotes the external allure more than the internal craving.

definition: Sweetness of sin; a theological phrase acknowledging the seductive pleasure of sexual transgression, used in Orthodox homiletics to explain why believers succumb and to underscore the mortal danger of carnal desire.
notes: Phrase from Orthodox homiletic and confessional literature. Notable for its phenomenological honesty: the сладость (sweetness/pleasure) is acknowledged as real, not dismissed, making the warning more sophisticated — the pleasure is the trap. Found in patristic texts translated into Church Slavonic and in 19th-century Russian religious writers.

definition: Flesh; in Orthodox and biblical usage, the corporeal nature of the human being with its appetites and passions — especially sexual desire — understood as the domain of carnal temptation opposed to the spirit.
notes: Church Slavonic word distinct from the neutral тело (body). The biblical antithesis плоть vs. дух (flesh vs. spirit) is foundational to Orthodox sexual ethics. Key collocations: грехи плоти (sins of the flesh), похоти плоти (lusts of the flesh), умерщвление плоти (mortification of the flesh). Not crude in itself — its gravity is theological.

definition: Mortification of the flesh; the Orthodox and broader Christian ascetic practice of deliberately suppressing bodily appetites — through fasting, cold exposure, sleep deprivation, and physical austerities — as a discipline against sexual desire and carnal passion.
notes: Умерщвление = 'killing off/deadening.' Goes well beyond sexual abstinence to include active physical self-punishment. Central to Orthodox monasticism and advocated in patristic ascetic literature (Evagrius, John Climacus). Mapped to sexual_abstinence as closest registry concept, though the practice is markedly more physically demanding and involves deliberate bodily suffering rather than mere restraint.

definition: Lustful or lascivious; an archaic adjective, influenced by Church Slavonic, applied to people, thoughts, or glances characterized by intense carnal sexual appetite.
notes: Archaic form; the modern equivalent is похотливый (same meaning, fully current). Derived from похоть (lust/carnal desire). Found primarily in religious texts, 18th–19th century literature, and deliberately archaizing registers. Recognition among speakers under 35 is low; older speakers recognize it readily from religious or literary exposure.

definition: Shameless; applied in Orthodox moral discourse and everyday Russian speech to someone — especially a woman — who displays sexual behavior without remorse, guilt, or social concealment, violating the shame-based norms that regulate sexuality.
notes: Literally без (without) + стыд (shame) → бесстыжий. Shame (стыд) functions as the primary internal regulator of sexual behavior in Russian honor-shame culture; бесстыжий names its absence. Applied with particular severity to women who display sexuality publicly or without apparent guilt. Still actively used in colloquial Russian — not archaic. The 'approximate' translation quality reflects that 'shameless' in English has largely lost its specifically sexual sting.

definition: Moral shame or sexual disgrace; in Orthodox usage also a euphemism for the genitals ('shameful parts').
notes: Derives from Proto-Slavic *sormŭ; in Church Slavonic and Orthodox homiletics. Phrase 'срамные места' = genitals.

definition: A disgraceful or shameful state of affairs, especially in sexual or moral matters; used exclamatorially to express moral outrage.
notes: Nominalised intensification of срам; exclamatory use predominates in folk and colloquial speech ('какая срамота!').

definition: Honor; in sexual contexts specifically a woman's chastity and sexual reputation as a socially enforced patriarchal and Orthodox moral value.
notes: Primary Russian word for honor in all senses; in sexual discourse means female chastity as a family-owned social commodity. Loss of честь is a central plot driver in 19th-century Russian literature.

definition: Dishonor; in sexual contexts the formal social category of a woman having lost her chastity and consequently her standing in community and family.
notes: Antonym of честь; a grave social and legal category in pre-Soviet Orthodox Russia. The concept frames sexual dishonor as an irreversible status change, not merely a reputation problem.

definition: Public disgrace or scandal; in sexual contexts the public humiliation of a person, especially a woman, for violating sexual norms.
notes: General-purpose word for shame/disgrace, not inherently sexual; mapped to slut_shaming here because in the honor-shame economy it functions as the mechanism of social enforcement against sexual transgressors.

definition: To publicly disgrace or shame someone, typically by exposing sexual misconduct or destroying their reputation.
notes: Perfective verb (single completed act of disgracing); can apply to any public dishonoring but is frequently used in sexual honor contexts.

definition: To disgrace oneself; to bring shame upon oneself through illicit or sexually indecent behavior.
notes: Reflexive counterpart of опозорить; the self-directed version of public sexual shaming; implies the subject's own conduct caused the disgrace.

definition: To stain or taint someone's honor; to destroy a woman's sexual reputation through seduction, rape, or public revelation of sexual misconduct.
notes: Metaphor of staining/sullying fabric; 'запятнать' = to spot, to blot; used in 19th-century literature and folk speech for sexual violation or scandal that destroys female honor.

definition: Slut, whore; the primary Russian crude insult for a sexually promiscuous woman.
notes: One of the most common sexual insults in Russian; used as a serious character attack and as casual hyperbole. Etymology uncertain; possibly from Polish 'szluja'. Near-mat register.

definition: A loose or promiscuous woman; literally 'the one who walks around (sexually)'; derived from гулять (to walk, to revel, to fool around).
notes: Traditional folk/colloquial pejorative; less offensive than шлюха but still stigmatizing. Also appears in historical and literary texts for women of easy virtue.

definition: To sleep around, to engage in promiscuous extramarital sex; literally 'to accumulate by walking/roving about.'
notes: Prefix на- = accumulative result; гулять = to walk/revel/fool around. Used in phrases like 'нагулялась в молодости' (she slept around in her youth). Always implies extramarital context.

definition: To conceive and bear a child out of wedlock through promiscuous sexual behavior; literally 'to walk a child into existence.'
notes: Extension of нагулять with direct object (ребёнка = child); always pejorative, attributing the pregnancy to the woman's promiscuity; the father is typically unnamed or unknown.

definition: Illegitimate; born outside of marriage; the formal legal and bureaucratic term for a bastard in pre-Soviet Russian civil and church law.
notes: Compound: незаконно (unlawfully) + рождённый (born); purely clinical/legal register with no inherent insult force, unlike байстрюк or бастард. Used in official documents and 19th-century literature.

definition: Bastard; a derogatory folk and dialectal term for an illegitimate child, used primarily in Ukrainian and South Russian speech.
notes: Primarily Ukrainian; enters Russian through Babel, Bulgakov, Southern dialects. Etymology disputed: possibly Polish 'bęckart' or Yiddish. Largely obsolete in contemporary standard Russian.

definition: Bastard; an illegitimate child or general insult for a contemptible person; a direct loanword from French/English.
notes: Used in historical (noble genealogy, heraldry) and literary contexts, and also as a general modern insult. Less emotionally loaded in Russian than in English; slightly bookish.

definition: A fallen woman; a woman who has lost her virtue through sexual sin; used in Orthodox moral discourse and 19th-century Russian literature.
notes: From пасть (to fall); strong Orthodox moral framing equating sexual sin with a spiritual fall from grace. Used by Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, et al. Not crude — literary and religiously charged. Russian equivalent of Victorian 'fallen woman'.

definition: A spoiled or corrupted woman; one who is no longer sexually pure or virtuous; used as a pejorative for a sexually experienced or morally compromised woman.
notes: Literally 'corrupted' or 'spoiled' (as food spoils); the sexual meaning is implicit and applied almost exclusively to women. The metaphor treats virginity as a commodity that degrades on contact.

definition: A slut; crude colloquial insult for a sexually promiscuous woman who is 'dragged around' between sexual partners.
notes: From потаскать/потащить (to drag around repeatedly); implies the woman has been physically passed from partner to partner. Diminutive suffix -ушка moderates form but not force.

definition: Whoring, gross sexual debauchery, promiscuity as a way of life; abstract noun derived from блядь (whore/slut); also used hyperbolically for any contemptible or dishonest conduct.
notes: Near-mat word; broad extended meaning covers any morally reprehensible behavior beyond sexuality ('это политическое блядство'). The -ство suffix makes it an abstract/collective concept rather than a single act.

definition: Shame; in the Russian sexual honor economy, the internalized negative affect that enforces sexual norms and polices individual behavior from within.
notes: Distinguished from позор (external public disgrace) by being internal and self-directed. 'Как не стыдно' (have you no shame?) is a primary social sanction. The Russian honor-shame system treats стыд and позор as complementary enforcement mechanisms.

definition: To shame oneself; to behave in a sexually or morally disgraceful manner; to make a public spectacle of one's own shameful conduct.
notes: Reflexive of срамить (to shame someone else); implies acting in a way that invites moral condemnation. More archaic than опозориться; primarily encountered in religious and folk literary contexts.

definition: A shameless woman; a woman who lacks sexual or moral shame and flaunts her behavior openly.
notes: Feminine noun; без-стыд-ница = without-shame-woman; less severe than шлюха; often used by older generations scolding younger women perceived as sexually immodest. Masculine form бесстыдник exists but is less charged.

definition: To dishonor someone; in historical and literary contexts specifically to rape or seduce a woman, thereby destroying her sexual honor and social standing irreversibly.
notes: From обес-честить (to strip of honor); in 19th-century Russian literature typically a euphemism for rape or seduction-unto-ruin. Cf. usage in Pushkin, Dostoevsky, Ostrovsky. Modern usage more broadly means to disgrace in any context.

definition: A girl's honor; the specific set phrase denoting female virginity and sexual purity as a socially and morally valued patriarchal commodity in Russian culture.
notes: Fixed phrase; 'защитить честь девушки' = to defend a girl's honor; 'лишить чести' = to take her honor. The concept frames female virginity as an asset belonging as much to the family as to the individual woman.

definition: Female breasts; slang term used in Russian criminal argot (fenya) and some informal colloquial speech.
notes: Origin unclear; possibly reduplicative baby-talk (childish diminutive pattern) or borrowed via Romani into fenya. Restricted primarily to fenya speakers and users of urban criminal slang; low recognition outside that subculture.

definition: A sexually promiscuous or loose woman; used as a harsh insult meaning slut or cheap prostitute in criminal argot and broad colloquial speech.
notes: Crossed from феня into general colloquial use; one of the most widely deployed Russian female-targeted sexual insults.

definition: Literally 'mare'; criminal argot for a large, coarse, or sexually available woman — dehumanizes by equine comparison.
notes: The horse metaphor implies both sexual availability and physical coarseness; in prison slang sometimes denotes a female inmate used as a sexual object by others.

definition: Intensified augmentative of сука (bitch); a maximally contemptuous insult for a vile or despicable woman.
notes: The -ара suffix is a pejorative intensifier; considerably stronger than сука alone; common in criminal argot and street speech.

definition: A whore or sexually promiscuous woman; a strong insult borrowed from Polish/Ukrainian kurwa.
notes: Loanword from Polish/Ukrainian; the foreign phonology can intensify its offensive edge in Russian; widely understood and used in Russian criminal speech.

definition: A vile, morally depraved, or nasty person; in criminal argot directed at women, implies sexual and moral corruption combined.
notes: Less specifically sexual than шалава; the sexual insult dimension emerges primarily from gendered application and context; also used for treacherous male figures.

definition: Literally 'hide/pelt/skin'; criminal argot for a sexually available woman or prostitute who sells herself.
notes: Dual meaning in феня: prostitute or sexually available woman AND informer/snitch — context determines which reading applies; both usages frame the person as something disposable.

definition: A girl or young woman (crude); literally 'heifer' (young female bovine); objectifying and mildly contemptuous but extremely widespread.
notes: Simplified spelling of тёлка (without ё); occupies a register similar to English 'chick' or British 'bird'; crude but not maximally offensive — also appears as entries 8 and 12 in this dataset.

definition: A girl or young woman (crude); literally 'heifer'; objectifying and mildly contemptuous but pervasive in colloquial Russian.
notes: Standard orthographic form (with ё); one of the most common crude-colloquial terms for a young woman in Russian; also appears as entries 7 and 12 in this dataset (simplified and repeated forms).

definition: Literally 'washcloth or bath loofah'; prison and criminal argot for a woman regarded purely as a sexual use-object to be worn down through repeated use.
notes: The washcloth metaphor is specifically apt: something used over and over until it deteriorates; more confined to criminal and prison environments than the other objectifying terms in this section.

definition: A woman who puts out readily; derived from давать (to give), the sexual idiom meaning to be sexually available; implies a promiscuous woman who never refuses.
notes: Transparent derivation from давать ('to give/put out'); the -алка suffix is an agent-noun suffix turning the verb into 'the one who gives (sex)'; always pejorative.

definition: Literally 'floor litter, bedding, or mat'; criminal argot for a woman who is laid down on by anyone — the image of a sexual doormat.
notes: Evokes something placed on the floor for anyone to walk on or lie upon; harsher and more specifically dehumanizing than тёлка in its denotative imagery.

definition: A girl or young woman (crude); literally 'heifer'; objectifying and mildly contemptuous. Duplicate entry — see entries 7 and 8.
notes: Third occurrence of this word in the source dataset; entries 7, 8, and 12 are all the same word in differing orthographic conventions (е vs. ё) or as a repeated item.

definition: Literally 'meat or flesh'; criminal argot that reduces women to raw sexual matter, the most extreme level of dehumanizing objectification.
notes: мясо also circulates in gaming and internet contexts ('пушечное мясо' = cannon fodder), reinforcing its sense of disposable material; in the sexual context the reduction is total.

definition: Literally 'frame/shot/cadre/personnel file'; criminal argot for a person — typically female — identified and marked as a candidate for sexual exploitation.
notes: In general Russian slang кадр means 'what a character/specimen'; the criminal-argot overlay frames the person as a personnel file to be acted upon — selected, assessed, and used.

definition: Sexual abuse perpetrated within the дедовщина system — the institutionalized caste-based hazing hierarchy of the Soviet and Russian military — by senior conscripts against junior ones.
notes: Дедовщина (from дед, 'grandfather/old timer') is a Soviet and post-Soviet military institution in which senior conscripts systematically abuse juniors across a rigid caste ladder; the sexual component uses rape and coercion to establish dominance and silence reporting through homophobic shame. No English term captures both the institutional caste structure and the sexual violence dimension simultaneously.

definition: Plural of дух ('spirit/ghost'); the lowest caste in the дедовщина military hierarchy — first-year conscripts subjected to labor, humiliation, and sexual abuse by senior soldiers.
notes: Also used as a term for enemy fighters (Afghan mujahideen, Chechen combatants) in military slang. In дедовщина contexts духи are the primary sexual victims. The ghost metaphor implies they are not yet fully real soldiers — and therefore not entitled to human dignity.

definition: Singular of духи; a single first-year conscript at the bottom of the дедовщина caste hierarchy, subject to sexual abuse and forced servitude by senior soldiers.
notes: Singular form of entry 16. Primary civilian meanings are 'spirit/soul' and 'scent/aroma'; the military hazing meaning is entirely register-specific.

definition: A raw, inexperienced military recruit or sailor; in дедовщина contexts, a novice conscript at or near the bottom of the hazing caste and therefore exposed to sexual and physical abuse.
notes: Originally navy slang — likely from a small worthless fish; migrated across all service branches. Functions more as a general insult for inexperience than a formally fixed caste rank in the way дух/духи is; overlap with that concept is strong.

definition: Literally 'young one'; in the дедовщина hierarchy, the second-year conscript rank — above духи but still subordinate to деды — both victim and perpetrator in the cycle of sexual hazing.
notes: The intermediate caste: молодые have survived their first year and are now entitled to victimize духи while remaining subject to the деды. This structural position perpetuates the cycle. No English concept captures the intermediate perpetrator-victim role in a military sexual-hazing caste hierarchy.

definition: To force or coerce; in дедовщина and criminal argot contexts, a euphemistic verb for compelling someone to perform a sexual act — i.e., rape or sexual coercion.
notes: The verb itself is neutral (to compel/force); the sexual meaning is entirely context-dependent. Used in дедовщина discourse as a distancing or legalistic euphemism for rape.

definition: Literally 'to lower or put down'; in Russian prison and criminal culture, to forcibly rape a man — typically anally — in order to permanently demote him to the опущенные caste, the irreversibly degraded stratum of the criminal hierarchy.
notes: One of the most culturally loaded concepts in Russian criminal culture. The act creates a permanent and irreversible caste change: the victim becomes опущенный ('lowered/degraded'), permanently untouchable and barred from normal social contact with other prisoners. No English concept captures both the specific act and the permanent social-caste consequence. The matching dедовщина usage transfers this prison logic into the military barracks context.

definition: A descriptive or meta phrase for homophobic slurs used in дедовщина contexts to shame sexually abused junior soldiers and prevent them from reporting abuse.
notes: A category label rather than a single slur; included in дедовщина sexual-hazing vocabulary because homophobic shaming is the primary silencing mechanism — perpetrators frame rape as making the victim gay, ensuring victims cannot report without identifying themselves as homosexual under Russia's hostile social and legal climate.

definition: One of the most powerful Russian mat phrases; literally '(I/he) fucked your mother'; deployed as an expression of extreme rage, contempt, or emphasis.
notes: Structurally parallel to English 'motherfucker' but second-person accusative ('your mother') rather than a compound noun. Part of core Russian мат — the highly restricted obscene register. Extremely pervasive in military speech; saying it to a superior can result in serious consequences; its frequency in barracks environments is near-constant.

definition: To curse at or verbally abuse someone using мат — the Russian system of strongly obscene language — as a form of aggression, dominance, or humiliation.
notes: Мат is a discrete register of Russian built around a small set of root words (хуй, пизда, ёб/ебать, блядь, etc.) with specific social rules governing permissible contexts. Материть is the transitive form — to direct мат AT a person rather than merely using profanity in general. Pervasive in дедовщина as an ongoing instrument of dominance; no English verb captures both the specific register system and the directional-abuse function.
